title: Fractions
summary: Fractions name equal parts; operations work by matching part sizes, counting parts, or asking how many fit.
idea:
A fraction names equal parts of a whole. In `3/4`, the bottom number says the whole is cut into four equal parts. The top number says three of those parts are taken.

The bottom number names the size of the parts. The top number counts how many parts there are.

Equivalent fractions name the same amount with different-sized parts. `1/2`, `2/4`, and `3/6` are the same amount. Multiplying or dividing the top and bottom by the same number keeps the amount the same.
why_it_works:
Fractions can be added only when the parts are the same size. For `1/2 + 1/3`, halves and thirds are changed into sixths first: `3/6 + 2/6`. Then the parts are the same size, so the counts can be added: `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`.

Multiplying by a fraction means taking that fraction of something. `3*(2/5)` means three lots of two fifths. The size of the parts stays fifths, and the count changes: `(3*2)/5` is `6/5`.

Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit. `(2/3)/(3/4)` becomes `(2/3)*(4/3)`, then `(2*4)/(3*3)`, which is `8/9`. The answer is less than one because `3/4` is a little more than `2/3`.

explanations.why: The fractions in `1/2 + 1/3` have different-sized parts, so they are not ready to add. The next move will rewrite them as equivalent fractions with the same bottom number.
explanations.another_way: Use a shared unit. Halves and thirds can both be cut into sixths, so each fraction can be renamed without changing its amount.
explanations.visual: A bar shows `1/2` shaded in halves and `1/3` shaded in thirds, with unequal part sizes.

explanations.why: Now both fractions are in sixths: `1/2` is `3/6`, and `1/3` is `2/6`. Since the parts are the same size, the top numbers can be counted together.
explanations.another_way: Think of it as `3` sixths plus `2` sixths. The unit stays sixths while the count of shaded parts is combined.
explanations.visual: A bar cut into `6` equal parts shows `3/6` shaded and another `2/6` shaded.

explanations.why: The total is `5/6` because `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`. This is the answer because the like-sized parts have been combined.
explanations.another_way: Count the shaded sixths in the bar model. There are `5` sixth-size parts shaded out of `6`.
explanations.visual: A bar cut into `6` equal parts has `5` parts shaded, showing `5/6`.

explanations.why: Multiplication by the whole number changes the count of fifths. In `3*(2/5)`, there are `3` groups of `2/5`.
explanations.another_way: Think of the move as repeated addition of equal fraction amounts. The same fraction size is used each time.
explanations.visual: A bar model shows `3` copies of a bar with `2/5` shaded in each copy.

explanations.why: This line shows that the numerators are multiplied while the denominator stays `5`. The size of each part is still fifths.
explanations.another_way: Count the fifths: `3` groups with `2` fifths in each group gives `(3*2)/5`.
explanations.visual: A bar model shows fifth-size pieces, with `3*2` of those pieces counted.

explanations.why: This is the answer because `3*2` is `6`, so `(3*2)/5` is `6/5`. It names the total number of fifths.
explanations.another_way: See the total as six fifth-size pieces, written as `6/5`.
explanations.visual: A bar model shows `6` fifth-size pieces shaded, making `6/5`.

explanations.why: The expression `(2/3)/(3/4)` asks how many `3/4` fit into `2/3`. Since `3/4` is a little bigger than `2/3`, the answer should be less than one.
explanations.another_way: Think of division as a fitting question: the size being fitted is `3/4`, and the amount available is `2/3`. This sets up why the result will be a fraction less than one whole.
explanations.visual: A bar of length `2/3` is compared with a bar of length `3/4`, which is slightly longer.

explanations.why: Dividing by `3/4` is changed to multiplying by its reciprocal, `4/3`. The dividend `2/3` stays the same; only the divisor is turned over.
explanations.another_way: Use the rule: keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and flip the second fraction. So `(2/3)/(3/4)` becomes `(2/3)*(4/3)`.
explanations.visual: The `2/3` bar stays in place while the `3/4` divisor is renamed by its reciprocal, `4/3`.

explanations.why: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. This writes `(2/3)*(4/3)` as `(2*4)/(3*3)`.
explanations.another_way: Count the parts in the numerators together and the part sizes in the denominators together. The product keeps numerator work over denominator work.
explanations.visual: A bar model shows `2` by `4` parts over `3` by `3` equal divisions.

explanations.why: The products in `(2*4)/(3*3)` give `8/9`. This is the answer because it is the simplified value reached by the fraction division steps.
explanations.another_way: The result `8/9` also matches the estimate: it is less than one, as expected because `3/4` is larger than `2/3`.
explanations.visual: A bar shows `8` of `9` equal parts shaded, a little less than one whole.

misconceptions.belief: To add fractions, add the tops and add the bottoms.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: It treats the fraction like two separate whole numbers, and it works the same way as multiplying fractions.

what_to_say.probe: Is your answer bigger or smaller than `1/2`? Should it be?
what_to_say.nudge: Can you add halves and thirds directly, or do you first need parts of the same size?
what_to_say.tell: Cut both into sixths: `3/6 + 2/6` is `5/6`. We only count the parts; their size stays the same.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students add fractions by adding the tops and adding the bottoms.

misconceptions.belief: To multiply a fraction by a whole number, multiply both the top and the bottom.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Students learned that doing the same to the top and the bottom is safe, from equivalent fractions.

what_to_say.probe: Is `6/15` more than `2/5`, less, or the same? What should three lots of `2/5` be?
what_to_say.nudge: Write three lots of two fifths as an addition and count the fifths.
what_to_say.tell: Three lots of two fifths is six fifths, `6/5`. Only the number of parts changes.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students multiply both the top and the bottom by the whole number.

misconceptions.belief: When dividing fractions, turn over the first fraction.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: "Flip and multiply" is remembered as a slogan without which fraction is flipped.

what_to_say.probe: How many three quarters fit into two thirds: more than one, or less?
what_to_say.nudge: Which fraction are we counting with? That is the one to turn over.
what_to_say.tell: Only the divisor is turned over: `(2/3)*(4/3)` is `8/9`, a little less than one.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students flip the first fraction when dividing, not the second.

misconceptions.belief: You can cancel a number on the top with the bottom even across a plus sign.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Cancelling common numbers works for products, and the student sees a 2 on the top and a 2 on the bottom.

what_to_say.probe: What is the top of the fraction altogether, before you divide?
what_to_say.nudge: Work out the top first, then divide. Do you get the same answer?
what_to_say.tell: The fraction bar divides the whole top: `(2+4)/2` is `6/2`, which is `3`.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students cancel across a plus sign.

misconceptions.belief: To simplify a fraction, you may divide just the top or just the bottom.
misconceptions.why_it_feels_right: Halving a number feels like simplifying, and the student does not check that the amount stays the same.

what_to_say.probe: Is `3/8` the same amount as `6/8`? Draw both as bars.
what_to_say.nudge: What number divides both the top and the bottom?
what_to_say.tell: Divide the top and the bottom by the same number: `6/8` is `3/4`.

misconceptions.source_quote: Some students simplify by changing only one part of the fraction.

questions.question: Why can’t the tops and bottoms just be added?
questions.answer: The bottom numbers name part sizes. Halves and thirds are different-sized parts, so they must be changed to the same size before adding.

questions.question: Why does `1/2 + 1/3` become `3/6 + 2/6`?
questions.answer: Both fractions are rewritten in sixths. That makes the parts the same size, so the counts can be added.

questions.question: Why is `3*(2/5)` not `6/15`?
questions.answer: Multiplying both top and bottom by `3` makes an equivalent fraction. It does not make three lots. Three lots of two fifths is `(3*2)/5`, which is `6/5`.

questions.question: Which fraction gets flipped in division?
questions.answer: Only the divisor is turned over. In `(2/3)/(3/4)`, the divisor is `3/4`, so the next step is `(2/3)*(4/3)`.

questions.question: Can cancelling happen across a plus sign?
questions.answer: No. The fraction bar applies to the whole top. For `(2+4)/2`, the top is `2+4`, so it becomes `6/2`, which is `3`.

questions.question: How can students check if a fraction answer makes sense?
questions.answer: Estimate first. Ask whether the answer should be more or less than one half or more or less than one. A quick size check catches many errors.

outline.title: Meaning of a fraction
outline.activity: Use `3/4` to name equal parts of a whole. Identify the bottom number as the size of the parts and the top number as the count of parts.

outline.title: Equivalent fractions
outline.activity: Compare `1/2`, `2/4`, and `3/6` as the same amount. Emphasize that changing both top and bottom by the same number keeps the value.

outline.title: Adding fractions
outline.activity: Work through `1/2 + 1/3`, then `3/6 + 2/6`, then `5/6`. Focus on making the parts the same size before counting them.

outline.title: Multiplying fractions by whole numbers
outline.activity: Interpret `3*(2/5)` as three lots of two fifths. Show `(3*2)/5`, then `6/5`. Stress that the part size stays fifths.

outline.title: Dividing by fractions
outline.activity: Use `(2/3)/(3/4)` to ask how many three-quarters fit into two thirds. Show `(2/3)*(4/3)`, `(2*4)/(3*3)`, and `8/9`.

outline.title: Estimate and catch errors
outline.activity: Discuss common errors: adding tops and bottoms, flipping the wrong fraction, cancelling across plus signs, and changing only one part of a fraction. Use estimation to check reasonableness.
